what_it_does: Network switches in data centers classify packets (decide where they should go) by comparing packet contents against thousands of rules simultaneously—a search that burns enormous power. This paper presents a specialized memory chip called a TCAM (ternary content-addressable memory) that does this pattern-matching in hardware. The innovation is selective search activation: instead of checking every rule in parallel and wasting power on rules that don't matter, the chip gates (turns on and off) search lines dynamically, checking only the relevant rules. A second optimization splits the memory array asymmetrically to scale power with the actual width of data being searched. Together these techniques save 37% of the power and reduce peak current spikes by nearly half, making network switching much more efficient.
